A.8 Debate-style dynamics and linear regret (Proofs for Sec. 3.4)

A.8.1 Persistent suboptimality under defensive mixing (Proof of Lem. 7)

We formalize a sufficient condition under which defensive mixing induces a persistent one-step advantage gap. The statement is deliberately worst-case: it isolates the mechanism (full-support mixing + nondegenerate gaps) and does not require the debate game to be zero-sum.

Modeling note.

In this subsection, each learning iteration kk corresponds to a single debate instance (one-shot stage), with public instance/state sks_{k} (e.g., prompt/context) and joint action 𝐚k=(aik,a−ik)\mathbf{a}^{k}=(a_{i}^{k},a_{-i}^{k}). Accordingly, πik(⋅∣sk)\pi_{i}^{k}(\cdot\mid s_{k}) is a mixed action (possibly depending on the public instance).

We interpret Qi⋆​(s,ai,a−i)Q_{i}^{\star}(s,a_{i},a_{-i}) as the true one-step action-value in the debate instance (equivalently the expected immediate payoff/score), with ⋆\star indicating that this is evaluated under the fixed reference environment defining the regret comparator (cf. Cor. 8).

Assumption 24 (Nondegenerate action-value gaps).

There exist constants Δgap>0\Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}>0 and qgap>0q_{\mathrm{gap}}>0, and an iteration k0k_{0}, such that for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0},

Pr⁡(maxai⁡Qi⋆​(sk,ai,a−ik)−minai⁡Qi⋆​(sk,ai,a−ik)≥Δgap)≥qgap.\Pr\Big(\max_{a_{i}}Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i},a_{-i}^{k})-\min_{a_{i}}Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i},a_{-i}^{k})\ \geq\ \Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}\Big)\ \geq\ q_{\mathrm{gap}}.
Assumption 25 (Persistent mixing).

There exist pmin>0p_{\min}>0 and an iteration k0k_{0} such that for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0} and all debate instances sks_{k},

πik​(ai∣sk)≥pmin∀ai∈𝒜i,\pi_{i}^{k}(a_{i}\mid s_{k})\geq p_{\min}\qquad\forall a_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i},

i.e., the learner maintains full support with a uniform lower bound (e.g., due to entropy regularization or forced exploration).

Proof of Lem. 7.

Fix k≥k0k\geq k_{0} and condition on (sk,a−ik)(s_{k},a_{-i}^{k}). Let

Mk:=maxai⁡Qi⋆​(sk,ai,a−ik).M_{k}:=\max_{a_{i}}Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i},a_{-i}^{k}).

Then, with aik∼πik(⋅∣sk)a_{i}^{k}\sim\pi_{i}^{k}(\cdot\mid s_{k}),

𝔼[Mk−Qi⋆(sk,aik,a−ik)|sk,a−ik]=Mk−∑aiπik(ai∣sk)Qi⋆(sk,ai,a−ik).\mathbb{E}\!\left[M_{k}-Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i}^{k},a_{-i}^{k})\ \big|\ s_{k},a_{-i}^{k}\right]=M_{k}-\sum_{a_{i}}\pi_{i}^{k}(a_{i}\mid s_{k})\,Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i},a_{-i}^{k}).

On the event in Assumption 24, there exists an action ai−a_{i}^{-} such that Qi⋆​(sk,ai−,a−ik)≤Mk−ΔgapQ_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i}^{-},a_{-i}^{k})\leq M_{k}-\Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}. By Assumption 25, πik​(ai−∣sk)≥pmin\pi_{i}^{k}(a_{i}^{-}\mid s_{k})\geq p_{\min}, hence

∑aiπik​(ai∣sk)​Qi⋆​(sk,ai,a−ik)≤(1−pmin)⋅Mk+pmin⋅(Mk−Δgap)=Mk−pmin​Δgap.\sum_{a_{i}}\pi_{i}^{k}(a_{i}\mid s_{k})\,Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i},a_{-i}^{k})\leq(1-p_{\min})\cdot M_{k}+p_{\min}\cdot(M_{k}-\Delta_{\mathrm{gap}})=M_{k}-p_{\min}\Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}.

Therefore,

𝔼[Mk−Qi⋆(sk,aik,a−ik)|sk,a−ik]≥pminΔgapon the nondegenerate-gap event.\mathbb{E}\!\left[M_{k}-Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i}^{k},a_{-i}^{k})\ \big|\ s_{k},a_{-i}^{k}\right]\geq p_{\min}\Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}\quad\text{on the nondegenerate-gap event}.

Taking expectation over (sk,a−ik)(s_{k},a_{-i}^{k}) yields

𝔼⁡[maxai⁡Qi⋆​(sk,ai,a−ik)−Qi⋆​(sk,aik,a−ik)]≥pmin​Δgap⋅qgap.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{a_{i}}Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i},a_{-i}^{k})\ -\ Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i}^{k},a_{-i}^{k})\right]\geq p_{\min}\Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}\cdot q_{\mathrm{gap}}.

Setting δmin:=pmin​Δgap​qgap>0\delta_{\min}:=p_{\min}\Delta_{\mathrm{gap}}\,q_{\mathrm{gap}}>0 concludes the proof. ∎

A.8.2 Linear Bayesian regret for MAD (Proof of Cor. 8)

The lemma above lower-bounds an ex-post advantage gap. To translate it into the welfare-based Bayesian regret in Eq. (2), we require a fixed comparator policy profile and a welfare objective aligned with the gap.

Assumption 26 (Stationary opponents after burn-in).

There exists k0k_{0} and a fixed opponent policy π−i⋆\pi_{-i}^{\star} such that for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}, the opponent action a−ika_{-i}^{k} is distributed according to π−i⋆(⋅∣sk)\pi_{-i}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s_{k}). Equivalently, π−ik≡π−i⋆\pi_{-i}^{k}\equiv\pi_{-i}^{\star} for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0} on the debate instances.

Assumption 27 (Welfare alignment for the regret comparator).

The welfare functional used in Eq. (2) is aligned with agent ii’s payoff in the debate instances: there exists a constant κ>0\kappa>0 such that for any two profiles that differ only in agent ii (with opponents fixed),

W⁡(πi′,π−i⋆)−W⁡(πi,π−i⋆)≥κ⋅(Ui​(πi′,π−i⋆)−Ui​(πi,π−i⋆)).W(\pi_{i}^{\prime},\pi_{-i}^{\star})-W(\pi_{i},\pi_{-i}^{\star})\ \geq\ \kappa\cdot\big(U_{i}(\pi_{i}^{\prime},\pi_{-i}^{\star})-U_{i}(\pi_{i},\pi_{-i}^{\star})\big).

A sufficient special case is a team/common-payoff debate objective where all agents share the same reward, in which case κ=N\kappa=N.

Assumption 28 (A fixed comparator attains the per-instance maximizer).

There exists a (possibly state-dependent) policy πi⋆(⋅∣s)\pi_{i}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s) such that for every debate instance ss and every opponent action a−ia_{-i} in the support of π−i⋆(⋅∣s)\pi_{-i}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s),

𝔼ai∼πi⋆(⋅∣s)[Qi⋆(s,ai,a−i)]=maxaiQi⋆(s,ai,a−i).\mathbb{E}_{a_{i}\sim\pi_{i}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s)}\big[Q_{i}^{\star}(s,a_{i},a_{-i})\big]\ =\ \max_{a_{i}}Q_{i}^{\star}(s,a_{i},a_{-i}).

In particular, this holds if there exists a measurable selector ai⋆​(s)a_{i}^{\star}(s) that is a maximizer for all such a−ia_{-i}, and πi⋆(⋅∣s)\pi_{i}^{\star}(\cdot\mid s) is the point mass at ai⋆​(s)a_{i}^{\star}(s).

Proof of Cor. 8.

Let 𝝅⋆:=(πi⋆,π−i⋆)\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star}:=(\pi_{i}^{\star},\pi_{-i}^{\star}) be the fixed comparator profile from Assumptions 26–28. By Assumption 28 and the definition of Qi⋆Q_{i}^{\star}, for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0},

Ui​(𝝅⋆)−Ui​(𝝅k)≥𝔼⁡[maxai⁡Qi⋆​(sk,ai,a−ik)−Qi⋆​(sk,aik,a−ik)].U_{i}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star})-U_{i}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\max_{a_{i}}Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i},a_{-i}^{k})\ -\ Q_{i}^{\star}(s_{k},a_{i}^{k},a_{-i}^{k})\right].

By Lem. 7, the right-hand side is at least δmin>0\delta_{\min}>0 for all k≥k0k\geq k_{0}. Applying Assumption 27 yields

W⁡(𝝅⋆)−W⁡(𝝅k)≥κ⋅(Ui​(𝝅⋆)−Ui​(𝝅k))≥κ​δmin∀k≥k0.W(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star})-W(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ \kappa\cdot\big(U_{i}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star})-U_{i}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\big)\ \geq\ \kappa\,\delta_{\min}\qquad\forall k\geq k_{0}.

Finally, under standard O⁡(1/k)O(1/\sqrt{k}) estimation errors, there exists k1k_{1} such that for all k≥k1k\geq k_{1} the additional loss attributable to estimation error is at most κ​δmin/2\kappa\delta_{\min}/2. (Equivalently, after k1k_{1} the policy is accurate enough that the persistent loss is dominated by the enforced mixing, not by estimation error.) Hence for all k≥k⋆:=max⁡{k0,k1}k\geq k_{\star}:=\max\{k_{0},k_{1}\},

W⁡(𝝅⋆)−W⁡(𝝅k)≥κ​δmin2=:c>0.W(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star})-W(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ \frac{\kappa\delta_{\min}}{2}\ =:c>0.

Therefore, for all T≥k⋆T\geq k_{\star},

RegretMAD​(T)=𝔼⁡[∑k=1T(W⁡(𝝅⋆)−W⁡(𝝅k))]≥∑k=k⋆Tc=Ω⁡(T).\mathrm{Regret}_{\mathrm{MAD}}(T)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{k=1}^{T}\big(W(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star})-W(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\big)\Big]\ \geq\ \sum_{k=k_{\star}}^{T}c\ =\ \Omega(T).

B.2 Weighted geometry: norm, Pinsker, and entropy curvature

Lemma 29 (Weighted block norm is a norm).

Assume weights wi​(hit,t)>0w_{i}(h_{i}^{t},t)>0 for all (i,hit,t)(i,h_{i}^{t},t) and ∑(hit,t)wi​(hit,t)=1\sum_{(h_{i}^{t},t)}w_{i}(h_{i}^{t},t)=1 for each ii. Then

∥𝝅−𝝅′∥1,2;w=(∑i∑(hit,t)wi(hit,t)∥πi(⋅∣hit,t)−πi′(⋅∣hit,t)∥12)1/2\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}=\Big(\sum_{i}\sum_{(h_{i}^{t},t)}w_{i}(h_{i}^{t},t)\,\|\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)-\pi_{i}^{\prime}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)\|_{1}^{2}\Big)^{1/2}

is a norm on Π\Pi.

Proof.

Nonnegativity and homogeneity are immediate. If ‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w=0\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}=0, then every summand is zero, hence πi(⋅∣hit,t)=πi′(⋅∣hit,t)\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)=\pi_{i}^{\prime}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t) for all (i,hit,t)(i,h_{i}^{t},t), so 𝝅=𝝅′\boldsymbol{\pi}=\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}. For the triangle inequality, let xi,u:=∥πi(⋅∣u)−πi′(⋅∣u)∥1x_{i,u}:=\|\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid u)-\pi_{i}^{\prime}(\cdot\mid u)\|_{1} with u=(hit,t)u=(h_{i}^{t},t). Then ‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w} is the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm (with weights) of the block vector (xi,u)(x_{i,u}), and Minkowski’s inequality yields the triangle inequality. ∎

Lemma 30 (Sup-to-block control).

If wi​(hit,t)≥wmin>0w_{i}(h_{i}^{t},t)\geq w_{\min}>0 and ∑(hit,t)wi​(hit,t)=1\sum_{(h_{i}^{t},t)}w_{i}(h_{i}^{t},t)=1, then for each fixed ii,

sup(hit,t)∥πi(⋅∣hit,t)−πi′(⋅∣hit,t)∥1≤wmin−1/2∥πi−πi′∥1,2;w.\sup_{(h_{i}^{t},t)}\|\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)-\pi_{i}^{\prime}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)\|_{1}\leq w_{\min}^{-1/2}\ \|\pi_{i}-\pi_{i}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}.

Let xu:=∥πi(⋅∣u)−πi′(⋅∣u)∥1x_{u}:=\|\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid u)-\pi_{i}^{\prime}(\cdot\mid u)\|_{1} with u=(hit,t)u=(h_{i}^{t},t). Then ∑uwi​(u)​xu2≥wmin​supuxu2\sum_{u}w_{i}(u)x_{u}^{2}\geq w_{\min}\sup_{u}x_{u}^{2}, hence supuxu≤wmin−1/2(∑uwi(u)xu2)1/2\sup_{u}x_{u}\leq w_{\min}^{-1/2}(\sum_{u}w_{i}(u)x_{u}^{2})^{1/2}. ∎

Lemma 31 (Weighted Pinsker).

For distributions p,qp,q on a finite alphabet and any α>0\alpha>0,

αKL(p∥q)≥α2∥p−q∥12,\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)\ \geq\ \frac{\alpha}{2}\,\|p-q\|_{1}^{2},

with the convention that KL(p∥q)=+∞\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)=+\infty if q⁡(a)=0q(a)=0 for some aa with p⁡(a)>0p(a)>0 (in which case the inequality is trivial). Hence if αi,t​(h)≥αmin>0\alpha_{i,t}(h)\geq\alpha_{\min}>0,

DΨ(𝝅,𝝅′)=∑i,t,hαi,t(h)wi(h,t)KL(πi∥πi′)≥αmin2∥𝝅−𝝅′∥1,2;w2.D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime})=\sum_{i,t,h}\alpha_{i,t}(h)\,w_{i}(h,t)\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{i}\|\pi_{i}^{\prime})\ \geq\ \frac{\alpha_{\min}}{2}\,\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.

Lemma 32 (Two-sided entropy curvature).

Let p,qp,q be distributions on a finite alphabet. If p,qp,q have full support (i.e. lie in the relative interior of the simplex), then

⟨∇(−ℋ)(p)−∇(−ℋ)(q),p−q⟩=KL(p∥q)+KL(q∥p)≥∥p−q∥12.\big\langle\nabla(-\mathcal{H})(p)-\nabla(-\mathcal{H})(q),\,p-q\big\rangle=\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)+\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\ \geq\ \|p-q\|_{1}^{2}.

In general (allowing zeros), the inequality KL(p∥q)+KL(q∥p)≥∥p−q∥12\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)+\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\geq\|p-q\|_{1}^{2} remains valid (with +∞+\infty interpreted in the usual way). Consequently,

∑i,t,hαi,t(h)wi(h,t)(KL(πi∥πi′)+KL(πi′∥πi))≥αmin∥𝝅−𝝅′∥1,2;w2.\sum_{i,t,h}\alpha_{i,t}(h)\,w_{i}(h,t)\,\big(\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{i}\|\pi_{i}^{\prime})+\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{i}^{\prime}\|\pi_{i})\big)\ \geq\ \alpha_{\min}\,\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.
Proof.

For full-support p,qp,q, ∇(−ℋ)​(p)=log⁡p+𝟏\nabla(-\mathcal{H})(p)=\log p+\mathbf{1} and the Bregman identity gives ⟨∇(−ℋ)(p)−∇(−ℋ)(q),p−q⟩=KL(p∥q)+KL(q∥p)\langle\nabla(-\mathcal{H})(p)-\nabla(-\mathcal{H})(q),p-q\rangle=\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)+\mathrm{KL}(q\|p). Applying Pinsker to both KL(p∥q)\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) and KL(q∥p)\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) yields KL(p∥q)+KL(q∥p)≥∥p−q∥12\mathrm{KL}(p\|q)+\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\geq\|p-q\|_{1}^{2}. When zeros occur, at least one KL term may be +∞+\infty, so the inequality still holds. Summing with weights αi,t​(h)​wi​(h,t)≥αmin​wi​(h,t)\alpha_{i,t}(h)w_{i}(h,t)\geq\alpha_{\min}w_{i}(h,t) gives the stated bound. ∎

B.3 QQ-sensitivity and a usable constant CQC_{Q}

Lemma 33 (QQ-sensitivity w.r.t. policy).

For all i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N} and joint policies 𝛑,𝛑~\boldsymbol{\pi},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}},

‖Qi𝝅−Qi𝝅~‖∞:=sup(hit,t),ai|Qi𝝅​(hit,ai,t)−Qi𝝅~​(hit,ai,t)|≤CQ​ρΠ​(𝝅,𝝅~),CQ:=2​Rmax(1−γ)2.\|Q_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}-Q_{i}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}}\|_{\infty}:=\sup_{(h_{i}^{t},t),a_{i}}\big|Q_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(h_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)-Q_{i}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}}(h_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)\big|\leq C_{Q}\,\rho_{\Pi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}),\qquad C_{Q}:=\frac{2R_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}.
Proof.

Let δ:=ρΠ​(𝝅,𝝅~)\delta:=\rho_{\Pi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}). Fix (i,hit,t,ai)(i,h_{i}^{t},t,a_{i}). Couple two future trajectories starting from the same time-tt joint configuration consistent with hith_{i}^{t} and taking the same prescribed aia_{i} for agent ii at time tt. Thereafter, couple the joint action draws step-by-step using maximal couplings of the joint action distributions induced by 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} and 𝝅~\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}. By definition of 𝖽Π\mathsf{d}_{\Pi}, at every step the probability that the coupled joint actions differ is at most δ\delta.

Let AmA_{m} be the event that at the mm-th future step (i.e. time t+mt+m) the coupled joint actions differ. Then Pr⁡(Am)≤δ\Pr(A_{m})\leq\delta for all m≥0m\geq 0. Let Em:=⋃j=0mAjE_{m}:=\bigcup_{j=0}^{m}A_{j} be the event that a disagreement has occurred at or before step mm. By a union bound, Pr⁡(Em)≤∑j=0mPr⁡(Aj)≤(m+1)​δ\Pr(E_{m})\leq\sum_{j=0}^{m}\Pr(A_{j})\leq(m+1)\delta.

If no disagreement has occurred up to step mm, then the coupled trajectories have identical states and joint actions at that step, hence identical rewards. Since rewards are bounded by RmaxR_{\max} in absolute value, the step-mm reward expectation difference is at most

|𝔼⁡[rt+m]−𝔼⁡[r~t+m]|≤2​Rmax​Pr⁡(Em)≤2​Rmax​(m+1)​δ.\big|\mathbb{E}[r_{t+m}]-\mathbb{E}[\tilde{r}_{t+m}]\big|\leq 2R_{\max}\Pr(E_{m})\leq 2R_{\max}(m+1)\delta.

Therefore,

|Qi𝝅​(hit,ai,t)−Qi𝝅~​(hit,ai,t)|≤∑m=0∞γm⋅2​Rmax​(m+1)​δ=2​Rmax​δ​∑m=0∞(m+1)​γm=2​Rmax(1−γ)2​δ.\big|Q_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(h_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)-Q_{i}^{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}}(h_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)\big|\leq\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{m}\cdot 2R_{\max}(m+1)\delta=2R_{\max}\delta\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(m+1)\gamma^{m}=\frac{2R_{\max}}{(1-\gamma)^{2}}\,\delta.

Taking the supremum over (hit,t),ai(h_{i}^{t},t),a_{i} yields the claim. ∎

B.4 Existence of HQRE (Proof of Thm. 10)

Lemma 34 (Logit map: well-definedness and continuity).

Assume αmin>0\alpha_{\min}>0. For any joint policy 𝛑\boldsymbol{\pi} and any (i,hit,t)(i,h_{i}^{t},t), the logit map ℬi𝛂(𝛑)(⋅∣hit,t)\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t) in Eq. (5) is a well-defined probability distribution on 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i}. Moreover, as a function of 𝛑\boldsymbol{\pi}, each ℬi𝛂\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} is continuous, and hence the joint logit map ℬ𝛂:Π→Π\mathcal{B}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}:\Pi\to\Pi is continuous on Π\Pi.

Proof.

Fix (i,hit,t)(i,h_{i}^{t},t). Since αi,t​(hit)≥αmin>0\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t})\geq\alpha_{\min}>0 and 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} is finite, the denominator in Eq. (5) is finite and strictly positive, so ℬi𝜶(𝝅)(⋅∣hit,t)\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t) is a valid distribution.

For continuity, Lemma 33 implies that Qi𝝅​(hit,⋅,t)Q_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(h_{i}^{t},\cdot,t) is Lipschitz (hence continuous) in 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} under ρΠ\rho_{\Pi}. For fixed αi,t​(hit)>0\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t})>0, the softmax map is smooth on ℝ|𝒜i|\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}_{i}|}. Composition yields continuity of each coordinate map ℬi𝜶\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, and therefore of ℬ𝜶\mathcal{B}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} under the product topology on Π\Pi. ∎

Proof of Thm. 10.

By Thm. 3, Π\Pi is nonempty, convex, compact, and metrizable. By Lemma 34, the joint logit map ℬ𝜶:Π→Π\mathcal{B}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}:\Pi\to\Pi is continuous. Schauder’s fixed-point theorem therefore yields a fixed point of ℬ𝜶\mathcal{B}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}} in Π\Pi, which is an HQRE by definition. ∎

Lemma 35 (Logit is TV-Lipschitz in QQ).

Fix (i,hit,t)(i,h_{i}^{t},t) and α:=αi,t​(hit)>0\alpha:=\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t})>0. For any x,y∈ℝ|𝒜i|x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{A}_{i}|},

TV⁡(softmax⁡(x/α),softmax⁡(y/α))≤12​α​‖x−y‖∞.\mathrm{TV}\!\big(\mathrm{softmax}(x/\alpha),\mathrm{softmax}(y/\alpha)\big)~\leq~\frac{1}{2\alpha}\,\|x-y\|_{\infty}.

‖p−q‖1≤supθ∈[0,1]‖Jϕ​(θ)‖∞→1​‖x−y‖∞,\|p-q\|_{1}\leq\sup_{\theta\in[0,1]}\|J_{\phi}(\theta)\|_{\infty\to 1}\,\|x-y\|_{\infty},

where the Jacobian of softmax(⋅/α)\mathrm{softmax}(\cdot/\alpha) at a probability vector rr is J⁡(r)=1α​(Diag⁡(r)−r​r⊤)J(r)=\tfrac{1}{\alpha}(\mathrm{Diag}(r)-rr^{\top}). ‖(Diag⁡(r)−r​r⊤)​v‖1=∑jrj​|vj−μ|=4​pS​(1−pS)≤1.\|(\mathrm{Diag}(r)-rr^{\top})v\|_{1}=\sum_{j}r_{j}|v_{j}-\mu|=4p_{S}(1-p_{S})\leq 1.

Thus ‖p−q‖1≤1α​‖x−y‖∞\|p-q\|_{1}\leq\tfrac{1}{\alpha}\|x-y\|_{\infty}, and dividing by 22 yields the TV bound. ∎

Fix 𝝅,𝝅~∈Π\boldsymbol{\pi},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\in\Pi and any joint history (ht,t)(h^{t},t). HQRE as a VI solution (standard in regularized games).

For completeness we record the usual variational-inequality characterization.

Lemma 37 (HQRE ⇔\Leftrightarrow VI solution).

Assume each Ji𝛂​(⋅,𝛑−i)J_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\cdot,\boldsymbol{\pi}_{-i}) is concave in πi\pi_{i} on Πi\Pi_{i} and differentiable, and that αmin>0\alpha_{\min}>0 so the regularized best response is single-valued. Then 𝛑⋆\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star} is an HQRE (fixed point of ℬ𝛂\mathcal{B}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}) if and only if it solves the VI:

find ​𝝅⋆∈Π​ s.t. ​⟨Freg​(𝝅⋆),𝝅−𝝅⋆⟩≥0,∀𝝅∈Π,\text{find }\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star}\in\Pi\text{ s.t. }\ \big\langle F_{\mathrm{reg}}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star}),\ \boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star}\big\rangle\geq 0,\quad\forall\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\Pi,

where Freg​(𝛑)=(−∇π1J1𝛂​(𝛑),…,−∇πNJN𝛂​(𝛑))F_{\mathrm{reg}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})=(-\nabla_{\pi_{1}}J_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi}),\ldots,-\nabla_{\pi_{N}}J_{N}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})).

Proof.

For concave differentiable games, a profile is a Nash equilibrium if and only if each player satisfies the first-order optimality condition ⟨−∇πiJi𝜶​(𝝅⋆),πi−πi⋆⟩≥0\langle-\nabla_{\pi_{i}}J_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star}),\ \pi_{i}-\pi_{i}^{\star}\rangle\geq 0 for all πi∈Πi\pi_{i}\in\Pi_{i}. Summing over ii yields the stated VI condition. With αmin>0\alpha_{\min}>0, each regularized best response is unique and is exactly the logit map ℬi𝜶\mathcal{B}_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, so Nash equilibrium is equivalent to the fixed-point condition defining HQRE. ∎

Proof of Thm. 12.

Recall Freg​(𝝅)=(−∇π1J1𝜶​(𝝅),…,−∇πNJN𝜶​(𝝅))F_{\mathrm{reg}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})=(-\nabla_{\pi_{1}}J_{1}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi}),\ldots,-\nabla_{\pi_{N}}J_{N}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})). Decompose each regularized payoff as Ji𝜶=Ui+Enti,𝜶J_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=U_{i}+\mathrm{Ent}_{i,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}, where

Enti,𝜶(𝝅)=𝔼𝝅[∑t≥0γtαi,t(hit)ℋ(πi(⋅∣hit,t))].\mathrm{Ent}_{i,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\Big[\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\,\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t})\,\mathcal{H}(\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t))\Big].

For the monotonicity calculation we only need the pointwise curvature of the negative-entropy term in each simplex component; this is captured by Lemma 32 and does not require any additional smoothness.

Step 1: unregularized part is LcL_{c}-hypomonotone.

By definition of LcL_{c} (Eq. (23)),

−∑i=1N⟨∇πiUi(𝝅)−∇πiUi(𝝅′),πi−πi′⟩≥−Lc∥𝝅−𝝅′∥1,2;w2.-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\langle\nabla_{\pi_{i}}U_{i}(\boldsymbol{\pi})-\nabla_{\pi_{i}}U_{i}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}),\,\pi_{i}-\pi_{i}^{\prime}\big\rangle\ \geq\ -\,L_{c}\,\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.
Step 2: entropy curvature contributes at least αmin\alpha_{\min}.

For every coordinate simplex (each (i,hit,t)(i,h_{i}^{t},t)), the negative entropy has two-sided curvature KL(πi∥πi′)+KL(πi′∥πi)≥∥πi−πi′∥12\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{i}\|\pi_{i}^{\prime})+\mathrm{KL}(\pi_{i}^{\prime}\|\pi_{i})\geq\|\pi_{i}-\pi_{i}^{\prime}\|_{1}^{2} (Lemma 32). Summing across coordinates with weights αi,t​(hit)​wi​(hit,t)≥αmin​wi​(hit,t)\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t})w_{i}(h_{i}^{t},t)\geq\alpha_{\min}w_{i}(h_{i}^{t},t) yields

−∑i=1N⟨∇πiEnti,𝜶(𝝅)−∇πiEnti,𝜶(𝝅′),πi−πi′⟩≥αmin∥𝝅−𝝅′∥1,2;w2.-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\langle\nabla_{\pi_{i}}\mathrm{Ent}_{i,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})-\nabla_{\pi_{i}}\mathrm{Ent}_{i,\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}),\,\pi_{i}-\pi_{i}^{\prime}\big\rangle\ \geq\ \alpha_{\min}\,\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.
Step 3: combine.

Adding the two bounds gives

⟨Freg​(𝝅)−Freg​(𝝅′),𝝅−𝝅′⟩≥(αmin−Lc)​‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w2,\big\langle F_{\mathrm{reg}}(\boldsymbol{\pi})-F_{\mathrm{reg}}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}),\,\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\big\rangle\geq(\alpha_{\min}-L_{c})\,\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2},

which is exactly the strong monotonicity claim.

If αmin>Lc\alpha_{\min}>L_{c}, then FregF_{\mathrm{reg}} is strongly monotone on Π\Pi and the VI solution is unique. By Lemma 37, this unique VI solution is exactly the unique HQRE.

Linear convergence of explicit mirror steps.

Let μ:=αmin−Lc>0\mu:=\alpha_{\min}-L_{c}>0. Under the additional field-Lipschitz and local-quadratic assumptions stated in Theorem 12, the linear-rate claim follows by applying Appendix Theorem 48 with F=FregF=F_{\mathrm{reg}}. This yields

DΨ​(𝝅⋆,𝝅k+1)≤ρ​DΨ​(𝝅⋆,𝝅k),ρ=1−η​μLΨ,D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1})\leq\rho\,D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\qquad\rho=1-\eta\,\frac{\mu}{L_{\Psi}},

for

0<η≤min⁡{μ​αmin2LF2​LΨ,αminLF}.0<\eta\leq\min\Big\{\frac{\mu\,\alpha_{\min}^{2}}{L_{F}^{2}L_{\Psi}},\,\frac{\alpha_{\min}}{L_{F}}\Big\}.

This is the exact rate quoted in Theorem 12. ∎

B.7 Zero-temperature limit (Proof of Lem. 13)

We first record two standard auxiliary inequalities that make the proof fully explicit.

Lemma 38 (Log-sum-exp (softmax) optimality gap).

Let x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and α>0\alpha>0, and let p=softmax⁡(x/α)∈Δdp=\mathrm{softmax}(x/\alpha)\in\Delta^{d}. Then for any q∈Δdq\in\Delta^{d},

⟨q,x⟩−⟨p,x⟩≤α​log⁡d.\langle q,x\rangle-\langle p,x\rangle\ \leq\ \alpha\log d.
Proof.

The softmax distribution pp is the unique maximizer of ⟨r,x⟩+α​ℋ​(r)\langle r,x\rangle+\alpha\mathcal{H}(r) over r∈Δdr\in\Delta^{d}. Thus for any qq,

⟨q,x⟩+α​ℋ​(q)≤⟨p,x⟩+α​ℋ​(p).\langle q,x\rangle+\alpha\mathcal{H}(q)\leq\langle p,x\rangle+\alpha\mathcal{H}(p).

Rearranging and using ℋ⁡(p)≤log⁡d\mathcal{H}(p)\leq\log d and ℋ⁡(q)≥0\mathcal{H}(q)\geq 0 yields ⟨q,x⟩−⟨p,x⟩≤α​log⁡d\langle q,x\rangle-\langle p,x\rangle\leq\alpha\log d. ∎

Lemma 39 (Discounted performance difference (one-player deviation)).

Fix ii and joint policies 𝛑=(πi,𝛑−i)\boldsymbol{\pi}=(\pi_{i},\boldsymbol{\pi}_{-i}) and 𝛑~=(π~i,𝛑−i)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=(\tilde{\pi}_{i},\boldsymbol{\pi}_{-i}). Then

Ui(π~i,𝝅−i)−Ui(𝝅)=11−γ𝔼(hit,t)∼𝖧discπ~i,𝝅−i[⟨π~i(⋅∣hit,t)−πi(⋅∣hit,t),Qi𝝅(hit,⋅,t)⟩].U_{i}(\tilde{\pi}_{i},\boldsymbol{\pi}_{-i})-U_{i}(\boldsymbol{\pi})=\frac{1}{1-\gamma}\,\mathbb{E}_{(h_{i}^{t},t)\sim\mathsf{H}_{\mathrm{disc}}^{\tilde{\pi}_{i},\boldsymbol{\pi}_{-i}}}\Big[\big\langle\tilde{\pi}_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)-\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t),\ Q_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(h_{i}^{t},\cdot,t)\big\rangle\Big].
Proof.

This is the standard discounted performance-difference identity obtained by unrolling UiU_{i} along the discounted visitation distribution of (π~i,𝝅−i)(\tilde{\pi}_{i},\boldsymbol{\pi}_{-i}) and expressing the per-step advantage in terms of Qi𝝅Q_{i}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}. A proof for finite spaces follows by conditioning on (hit,t)(h_{i}^{t},t), writing the one-step deviation advantage at (hit,t)(h_{i}^{t},t), and summing the resulting telescoping series under the geometric discount. ∎

Proof of Lem. 13.

By Thm. 3, Π\Pi is compact, so {𝝅(n)}\{\boldsymbol{\pi}^{(n)}\} admits a convergent subsequence (not relabeled) with limit 𝝅¯\bar{\boldsymbol{\pi}}.

B.8 Hierarchical definitions and composite KL geometry

We make the Local–Global HQRE construction explicit and fix notation to match the main text (zz is the public context).

Spaces.

Let ΠCk=∏i∈CkΠi\Pi_{C_{k}}=\prod_{i\in C_{k}}\Pi_{i} and Πclu=∏k=1KΠCk\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}}=\prod_{k=1}^{K}\Pi_{C_{k}}. Let 𝒢=∏z∈𝒵ΔK\mathcal{G}=\prod_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\Delta^{K} denote the gate space. Under (A1)–(A2), Πclu\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}} and 𝒢\mathcal{G} are compact, convex, and metrizable (finite/countable products of simplices).

Gate objective and softmax update.

Given 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi}, define the context-conditional cluster score

Q~loc,c𝝅(z):=𝔼t∼Geom⁡(1−γ)𝔼𝐚Cc∼𝝅Cc(⋅∣z,t)[Q¯loc,c(z,𝐚Cc,t)],\widetilde{Q}_{\mathrm{loc},c}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(z):=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathrm{Geom}(1-\gamma)}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a}_{C_{c}}\sim\boldsymbol{\pi}_{C_{c}}(\cdot\mid z,t)}\big[\bar{Q}_{\mathrm{loc},c}(z,\mathbf{a}_{C_{c}},t)\big],

where Q¯loc,c\bar{Q}_{\mathrm{loc},c} is as in Eq. (12). For each zz, the gate solves the strictly concave problem

maxg⁡(z)∈ΔK∑c=1Kgc(z)Q~loc,c𝝅(z)+τgℋ(g(⋅∣z)).\max_{g(z)\in\Delta^{K}}\ \sum_{c=1}^{K}g_{c}(z)\,\widetilde{Q}_{\mathrm{loc},c}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(z)\ +\ \tau_{g}\,\mathcal{H}(g(\cdot\mid z)).

Its unique maximizer is

gc⋆​(z)∝exp⁡(Q~loc,c𝝅​(z)/τg),g_{c}^{\star}(z)\ \propto\ \exp\!\big(\widetilde{Q}_{\mathrm{loc},c}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(z)/\tau_{g}\big),

and the map 𝝅↦g⋆\boldsymbol{\pi}\mapsto g^{\star} is continuous as a composition of continuous maps.

Composite divergence and norm.

Define the composite KL divergence

DΨhier((𝝅,g),(𝝅′,g′)):=DΨ(𝝅,𝝅′)+τg∑z∈𝒵KL(g(⋅∣z)∥g′(⋅∣z)).D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}((\boldsymbol{\pi},g),(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime},g^{\prime})):=D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime})\ +\ \tau_{g}\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\mathrm{KL}(g(\cdot\mid z)\,\|\,g^{\prime}(\cdot\mid z)).

Define the associated composite ℓ1,2\ell_{1,2}-type norm

∥(𝝅,g)−(𝝅′,g′)∥hier2:=∥𝝅−𝝅′∥1,2;w2+∑z∈𝒵∥g(⋅∣z)−g′(⋅∣z)∥12.\|(\boldsymbol{\pi},g)-(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime},g^{\prime})\|_{\mathrm{hier}}^{2}:=\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}\ +\ \sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\|g(\cdot\mid z)-g^{\prime}(\cdot\mid z)\|_{1}^{2}.

By Lemma 31 (for 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi}) and Pinsker for the gate component,

DΨhier​((𝝅,g),(𝝅′,g′))≥min⁡{αmin,τg}2​‖(𝝅,g)−(𝝅′,g′)‖hier2.D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}((\boldsymbol{\pi},g),(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime},g^{\prime}))\ \geq\ \frac{\min\{\alpha_{\min},\tau_{g}\}}{2}\ \|(\boldsymbol{\pi},g)-(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime},g^{\prime})\|_{\mathrm{hier}}^{2}. (25)

B.9 Hierarchical existence (Proof of Thm. 15)

Proof of Thm. 15.

Under (A1)–(A2), the space Πclu×𝒢\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}}\times\mathcal{G} is nonempty, convex, compact, and metrizable. Assume αmin>0\alpha_{\min}>0 and τg>0\tau_{g}>0.

For execution agents, define the block logit map on Πclu\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}} as the product of the per-agent logit responses Eq. (5); by Lemma 34 it is continuous and maps Πclu\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}} to itself. For the gate, Appendix B.8 shows that for each 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} the best-response gate g⋆​(𝝅)g^{\star}(\boldsymbol{\pi}) is single-valued and continuous.

Define the joint map

𝒯⁡(𝝅,g):=(ℬ𝜶​(𝝅),g⋆​(𝝅)),(𝝅,g)∈Πclu×𝒢.\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{\pi},g):=\big(\mathcal{B}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{\pi}),\ g^{\star}(\boldsymbol{\pi})\big),\qquad(\boldsymbol{\pi},g)\in\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}}\times\mathcal{G}.

Then 𝒯\mathcal{T} is continuous and maps the compact convex set Πclu×𝒢\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}}\times\mathcal{G} to itself. By Schauder’s fixed-point theorem, 𝒯\mathcal{T} has a fixed point (𝝅⋆,g⋆)(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star},g^{\star}), which is by definition a Local–Global HQRE. ∎

B.11 Hierarchical strong monotonicity and explicit KL–prox linear rate (Proof of Thm. 17)

Proof of Thm. 17.

Let the hierarchical variable be 𝐳=(𝝅,g)∈Πclu×𝒢\mathbf{z}=(\boldsymbol{\pi},g)\in\Pi_{\mathrm{clu}}\times\mathcal{G} and use the composite divergence DΨhierD_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}} from Appendix B.8. DΨhier​(𝐳⋆,𝐳k+1)≤(1−η​μhierLΨhier)​DΨhier​(𝐳⋆,𝐳k),D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}(\mathbf{z}^{\star},\mathbf{z}^{k+1})\leq\Big(1-\eta\,\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{hier}}}{L_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}}\Big)D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}(\mathbf{z}^{\star},\mathbf{z}^{k}),

This appendix collects proofs for the learning–dynamics results summarized in Table 15: the ELBO / best-response-gap equivalence (Prop. 42), monotone progress of KL–mirror steps (Thm. 46), linear convergence of KL–mirror dynamics in the strongly monotone regime (Thm. 48), and their hierarchical counterparts (Thm. 52). We also prove the soft-value factorization and weighted-advantage identities (Prop. 44, Lem. 45) used in Sec. 5.3.

Local discounted occupancy over information states.

For a joint policy 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi}, define the discounted occupancy measure on player ii’s information states ℐi={(hit,t)}\mathcal{I}_{i}=\{(h_{i}^{t},t)\} by

𝖧i,disc𝝅​(hit,t):=(1−γ)​γt​Pr𝝅⁡(hit),\mathsf{H}_{i,\mathrm{disc}}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(h_{i}^{t},t):=(1-\gamma)\gamma^{t}\,\Pr_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}(h_{i}^{t}),

∑t≥0γt​𝔼𝝅​[f⁡(hit,t)]=(1−γ)−1​𝔼(hit,t)∼𝖧i,disc𝝅​[f⁡(hit,t)].\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\,\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\pi}}[f(h_{i}^{t},t)]=(1-\gamma)^{-1}\,\mathbb{E}_{(h_{i}^{t},t)\sim\mathsf{H}_{i,\mathrm{disc}}^{\boldsymbol{\pi}}}[f(h_{i}^{t},t)].

C.1 ELBO decomposition and best-response gaps (Prop. 42)

(26)

Lemma 43 (One-step ELBO identity).

Fix an information state (hit,t)(h_{i}^{t},t) and a temperature α:=αi,t​(hit)>0\alpha:=\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t})>0. Let q⁡(a)=Qiπi⋆​(hit,a,t)q(a)=Q_{i}^{\pi_{i}^{\star}}(h_{i}^{t},a,t) and let p⋆(⋅∣hit,t)=softmax(q(⋅)/α)p^{\star}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)=\mathrm{softmax}(q(\cdot)/\alpha), i.e.,

p⋆​(ai∣hit,t)∝exp⁡(Qiπi⋆​(hit,ai,t)/αi,t​(hit)).p^{\star}(a_{i}\mid h_{i}^{t},t)\propto\exp\!\big(Q_{i}^{\pi_{i}^{\star}}(h_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)/\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t})\big).

Then for any p∈Δ⁡(𝒜i)p\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}_{i}),

∑aip(ai)q(ai)+αℋ(p)=αlog∑aiexp(q(ai)/α)−αKL(p∥p⋆).\sum_{a_{i}}p(a_{i})\,q(a_{i})+\alpha\,\mathcal{H}(p)=\alpha\log\sum_{a_{i}}\exp\!\big(q(a_{i})/\alpha\big)-\alpha\,\mathrm{KL}(p\|p^{\star}).
Proof.

This is the standard log-sum-exp / convex conjugacy identity. Let α=αi,t​(hit)\alpha=\alpha_{i,t}(h_{i}^{t}), q⁡(a)=Qiπi⋆​(hit,a,t)q(a)=Q_{i}^{\pi_{i}^{\star}}(h_{i}^{t},a,t), and Z=∑aexp⁡(q⁡(a)/α)Z=\sum_{a}\exp(q(a)/\alpha). Define p⋆​(a)=exp⁡(q⁡(a)/α)/Zp^{\star}(a)=\exp(q(a)/\alpha)/Z. Then

The RHS in Eq. (26) is nonnegative and equals 00 iff πi(⋅∣hit,t)=πi⋆(⋅∣hit,t)\pi_{i}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t)=\pi_{i}^{\star}(\cdot\mid h_{i}^{t},t) for 𝖧i,disc(πi,𝝅−i)\mathsf{H}_{i,\mathrm{disc}}^{(\pi_{i},\boldsymbol{\pi}_{-i})}-a.e. information state, so πi⋆\pi_{i}^{\star} is the unique maximizer. Finally, a joint profile is a Nash equilibrium of the regularized game iff each player is at its unique regularized best response, which is equivalent to being a joint fixed point of the logit map ℬ𝜶\mathcal{B}^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}. ∎

C.2 Soft-value factorization and weighted advantages

Proposition 44 (Soft-value factorization).

Assume a linear monotone mixer of the form

Qtot​(st,𝐚t,t)=∑i=1Nwi​(st)​Qi​(bit,ait,t)+b⁡(st),wi​(st)≥0,Q_{\mathrm{tot}}(s^{t},\mathbf{a}^{t},t)=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}(s^{t})\,Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i}^{t},t)+b(s^{t}),\qquad w_{i}(s^{t})\geq 0,

and a scalar temperature αt>0\alpha_{t}>0. Define the exact total soft value

Vtotexact​(st,t):=αt​log​∑𝐚texp⁡(Qtot​(st,𝐚t,t)/αt).V_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(s^{t},t):=\alpha_{t}\log\sum_{\mathbf{a}^{t}}\exp\big(Q_{\mathrm{tot}}(s^{t},\mathbf{a}^{t},t)/\alpha_{t}\big).

Then it factorizes as

Vtotexact(st,t)=b(st)+αt∑i=1Nlog∑ai∈𝒜iexp(wi​(st)αtQi(bit,ai,t)).V_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(s^{t},t)=b(s^{t})+\alpha_{t}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\sum_{a_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{i}}\exp\Big(\tfrac{w_{i}(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}\,Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)\Big). (29)

This is the algebraic identity instantiated as Eq. (29) in Sec. 5.3 (with aia_{i} replaced by vocabulary tokens and tt replaced by token positions ℓ\ell).

Proof.

By definition,

Qtot​(st,𝐚t,t)αt=b⁡(st)αt+∑i=1Nwi​(st)αt​Qi​(bit,ait,t).\frac{Q_{\mathrm{tot}}(s^{t},\mathbf{a}^{t},t)}{\alpha_{t}}=\frac{b(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}+\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{w_{i}(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}\,Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i}^{t},t).

Hence

∑𝐚texp⁡(Qtot​(st,𝐚t,t)αt)\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{a}^{t}}\exp\!\Big(\frac{Q_{\mathrm{tot}}(s^{t},\mathbf{a}^{t},t)}{\alpha_{t}}\Big) =exp(b(st)/αt)∑a1⋯∑aNexp(∑i=1Nwi​(st)αtQi(bit,ait,t))\displaystyle=\exp\!\big(b(s^{t})/\alpha_{t}\big)\,\sum_{a_{1}}\cdots\sum_{a_{N}}\exp\!\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tfrac{w_{i}(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}\,Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i}^{t},t)\Big)
=exp⁡(b⁡(st)/αt)​∏i=1N∑aiexp⁡(wi​(st)αt​Qi​(bit,ai,t)),\displaystyle=\exp\!\big(b(s^{t})/\alpha_{t}\big)\,\prod_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{a_{i}}\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{w_{i}(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}\,Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)\Big),

since the exponent separates across ii. Taking αt​log⁡(⋅)\alpha_{t}\log(\cdot) yields the claim. ∎

Lemma 45 (Weighted local soft values and soft advantages).

Assume αt>0\alpha_{t}>0 and wi​(st)>0w_{i}(s^{t})>0 for the indices ii under consideration.55 5 If wi​(st)=0w_{i}(s^{t})=0 then the ii-th term does not contribute to QtotQ_{\mathrm{tot}}; one can define wi​(st)​Visoft:=αt​log​∑aiexp⁡((wi/αt)​Qi)w_{i}(s^{t})V_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}:=\alpha_{t}\log\sum_{a_{i}}\exp((w_{i}/\alpha_{t})Q_{i}) and all identities remain valid. Define the local soft value

Visoft​(st,bit,t):=αtwi​(st)​log​∑aiexp⁡(wi​(st)αt​Qi​(bit,ai,t)),V_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}(s^{t},b_{i}^{t},t):=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{w_{i}(s^{t})}\log\sum_{a_{i}}\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{w_{i}(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}\,Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)\Big),

Ai(w)​(st,bit,ait,t):=wi​(st)​(Qi​(bit,ait,t)−Visoft​(st,bit,t)).A_{i}^{(w)}(s^{t},b_{i}^{t},a_{i}^{t},t):=w_{i}(s^{t})\Big(Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i}^{t},t)-V_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}(s^{t},b_{i}^{t},t)\Big).

Then:

  1. (i)

    Vtotexact​(st,t)=b⁡(st)+∑i=1Nwi​(st)​Visoft​(st,bit,t)V_{\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{exact}}(s^{t},t)=b(s^{t})+\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}(s^{t})V_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}(s^{t},b_{i}^{t},t).

  2. (ii)

    For the softmax policy πisoft​(ai∣bit,t)∝exp⁡(wi​(st)αt​Qi​(bit,ai,t))\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}(a_{i}\mid b_{i}^{t},t)\propto\exp(\tfrac{w_{i}(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)), the advantage admits the pointwise identity

    Ai(w)​(st,bit,ait,t)=αt​log⁡πisoft​(ait∣bit,t),A_{i}^{(w)}(s^{t},b_{i}^{t},a_{i}^{t},t)=\alpha_{t}\,\log\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}(a_{i}^{t}\mid b_{i}^{t},t),

    𝔼ai∼πisoft[Ai(w)(st,bit,ai,t)]=−αtℋ(πisoft(⋅∣bit,t)).\mathbb{E}_{a_{i}\sim\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}}\!\big[A_{i}^{(w)}(s^{t},b_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)\big]=-\alpha_{t}\,\mathcal{H}\big(\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}(\cdot\mid b_{i}^{t},t)\big).

(i) follows by substituting the definition of VisoftV_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}} into Prop. 44.

(ii) Let Zi:=∑aiexp⁡(wiαt​Qi​(bit,ai,t))Z_{i}:=\sum_{a_{i}}\exp(\tfrac{w_{i}}{\alpha_{t}}Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)). Then

log⁡πisoft​(ai∣bit,t)=wi​(st)αt​Qi​(bit,ai,t)−log⁡Zi.\log\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}(a_{i}\mid b_{i}^{t},t)=\tfrac{w_{i}(s^{t})}{\alpha_{t}}Q_{i}(b_{i}^{t},a_{i},t)-\log Z_{i}.

which is exactly Ai(w)A_{i}^{(w)}. Taking expectation under πisoft\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}} yields 𝔼⁡[log⁡πisoft]=−ℋ⁡(πisoft)\mathbb{E}[\log\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}]=-\mathcal{H}(\pi_{i}^{\mathrm{soft}}) and hence the last identity. ∎

C.3 Monotone progress for KL–mirror steps (Thm. 46)

We provide a clean mirror-ascent progress bound in KL geometry.

Theorem 46 (Monotone progress of KL–mirror ascent).

Let J:Π→ℝJ:\Pi\to\mathbb{R} be differentiable and LJL_{J}-smooth in the ∥⋅∥1,2;w\|\cdot\|_{1,2;w} norm, i.e., for all 𝛑,𝛑′∈Π\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\in\Pi,

J⁡(𝝅′)≥J⁡(𝝅)+⟨∇J​(𝝅),𝝅′−𝝅⟩−LJ2​‖𝝅′−𝝅‖1,2;w2.J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime})\ \geq\ J(\boldsymbol{\pi})+\langle\nabla J(\boldsymbol{\pi}),\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}-\boldsymbol{\pi}\rangle-\frac{L_{J}}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}-\boldsymbol{\pi}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.

Assume the KL–Bregman divergence DΨD_{\Psi} (Eq. (7)) satisfies the weighted Pinsker lower bound DΨ​(𝛑,𝛑′)≥αmin2​‖𝛑−𝛑′‖1,2;w2D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime})\geq\frac{\alpha_{\min}}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2} (as in Lem. 31). Consider the KL–mirror ascent step

𝝅k+1=arg⁡max𝝅~∈Π​{⟨∇J​(𝝅k),𝝅~−𝝅k⟩−1ηk​DΨ​(𝝅~,𝝅k)}.\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1}=\arg\max_{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\in\Pi}\Big\{\langle\nabla J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}\rangle-\tfrac{1}{\eta_{k}}D_{\Psi}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\Big\}. (30)

If ηk≤αmin/(2​LJ)\eta_{k}\leq\alpha_{\min}/(2L_{J}), then

J⁡(𝝅k+1)−J⁡(𝝅k)≥12​ηk​DΨ​(𝝅k+1,𝝅k)≥ 0.J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1})-J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ \frac{1}{2\eta_{k}}\,D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ 0.
Lemma 47 (Mirror optimality inequality).

For the update Eq. (30),

⟨∇J​(𝝅k),𝝅k+1−𝝅k⟩≥1ηk​DΨ​(𝝅k+1,𝝅k).\langle\nabla J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}\rangle\geq\frac{1}{\eta_{k}}D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}).
Proof.

Since 𝝅~=𝝅k\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}=\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k} is feasible, optimality of 𝝅k+1\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1} implies

⟨∇J​(𝝅k),𝝅k+1−𝝅k⟩−1ηk​DΨ​(𝝅k+1,𝝅k)≥ 0,\langle\nabla J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}\rangle-\tfrac{1}{\eta_{k}}D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ 0,

which yields the claim. ∎

Proof of Thm. 46.

By LJL_{J}-smoothness applied with 𝝅=𝝅k\boldsymbol{\pi}=\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k} and 𝝅′=𝝅k+1\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1},

J⁡(𝝅k+1)−J⁡(𝝅k)≥⟨∇J​(𝝅k),𝝅k+1−𝝅k⟩−LJ2​‖𝝅k+1−𝝅k‖1,2;w2.J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1})-J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\geq\langle\nabla J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}\rangle-\frac{L_{J}}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.

Use Lem. 47 and the Pinsker lower bound to obtain

If ηk≤αmin/(2​LJ)\eta_{k}\leq\alpha_{\min}/(2L_{J}), then 1ηk−LJαmin≥12​ηk\frac{1}{\eta_{k}}-\frac{L_{J}}{\alpha_{\min}}\geq\frac{1}{2\eta_{k}}, hence

J⁡(𝝅k+1)−J⁡(𝝅k)≥12​ηk​DΨ​(𝝅k+1,𝝅k)≥ 0.J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1})-J(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ \frac{1}{2\eta_{k}}\,D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\ \geq\ 0.

C.4 Linear convergence in KL geometry (Thm. 48)

We now give a self-contained linear-rate bound for KL–mirror dynamics in the strongly monotone regime. The argument is standard but we spell out the key inequalities and constants needed for a publishable statement.

Theorem 48 (Linear convergence of KL–mirror dynamics).

Let F:Π→𝒳F:\Pi\to\mathcal{X} be a field and suppose the variational inequality VI⁡(F,Π)\mathrm{VI}(F,\Pi) has a unique solution 𝛑⋆\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star} (e.g., when FF is strongly monotone). Assume:

  1. (i)

    (Strong monotonicity) There exists μ>0\mu>0 such that for all 𝝅,𝝅′∈Π\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\in\Pi,

    ⟨F⁡(𝝅)−F⁡(𝝅′),𝝅−𝝅′⟩≥μ​‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w2.\langle F(\boldsymbol{\pi})-F(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}),\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\rangle\geq\mu\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.
  2. (ii)

    (Lipschitzness) There exists LF<∞L_{F}<\infty such that

    ‖F⁡(𝝅)−F⁡(𝝅′)‖∗≤LF​‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w,\|F(\boldsymbol{\pi})-F(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime})\|_{\ast}\leq L_{F}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w},

    where ∥⋅∥∗\|\cdot\|_{\ast} is the dual norm of ∥⋅∥1,2;w\|\cdot\|_{1,2;w}.

  3. (iii)

    (Local quadratic KL geometry) There exists LΨ<∞L_{\Psi}<\infty such that for all 𝝅,𝝅′\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime} in a neighborhood containing 𝝅⋆\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star} and the iterates,

    αmin2​‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w2≤DΨ​(𝝅,𝝅′)≤LΨ2​‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w2.\frac{\alpha_{\min}}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}\ \leq\ D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime})\ \leq\ \frac{L_{\Psi}}{2}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.

    A sufficient condition is iterate-interiority: if every local action probability in that region is bounded below by νmin>0\nu_{\min}>0, then one may take LΨ=αmax/νminL_{\Psi}=\alpha_{\max}/\nu_{\min}.

Consider the mirror step for VI⁡(F,Π)\mathrm{VI}(F,\Pi):

𝝅k+1=arg⁡min𝝅~∈Π​{⟨F⁡(𝝅k),𝝅~−𝝅k⟩+1η​DΨ​(𝝅~,𝝅k)}.\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1}=\arg\min_{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}\in\Pi}\Big\{\langle F(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}\rangle+\tfrac{1}{\eta}D_{\Psi}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\pi}},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\Big\}. (31)

If the stepsize satisfies

0<η≤min⁡{μ​αmin2LF2​LΨ,αminLF},0<\eta\ \leq\ \min\Big\{\frac{\mu\,\alpha_{\min}^{2}}{L_{F}^{2}\,L_{\Psi}},\ \frac{\alpha_{\min}}{L_{F}}\Big\},

then the iterates converge linearly in KL geometry:

DΨ​(𝝅⋆,𝝅k+1)≤ρ​DΨ​(𝝅⋆,𝝅k),ρ:=1−η​μLΨ∈(0,1).D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1})\leq\rho\,D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\star},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\qquad\rho:=1-\eta\,\frac{\mu}{L_{\Psi}}\ \in(0,1).
Remark 49 (Why the KL upper quadratic bound is local).

For entropy / KL mirror maps, the lower quadratic bound is global but the upper quadratic bound is only local on the simplex. If all policies in the iterate region satisfy πi​(a∣h,t)≥νmin>0\pi_{i}(a\mid h,t)\geq\nu_{\min}>0 for every relevant coordinate, then the Hessian of the negative-entropy mirror map is bounded above by 1/νmin1/\nu_{\min} coordinatewise, yielding

DΨ​(𝝅,𝝅′)≤αmax2​νmin​‖𝝅−𝝅′‖1,2;w2.D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime})\leq\frac{\alpha_{\max}}{2\nu_{\min}}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}-\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\prime}\|_{1,2;w}^{2}.

Practically, DICE-FT promotes this interior regime via positive entropies, KL trust regions, and step rejection.

Lemma 50 (Three-point inequality for VI mirror steps).

Let 𝛑k+1\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1} be defined by Eq. (31). Then for any 𝛑∈Π\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\Pi,

⟨F⁡(𝝅k),𝝅k+1−𝝅⟩≤1η​(DΨ​(𝝅,𝝅k)−DΨ​(𝝅,𝝅k+1)−DΨ​(𝝅k+1,𝝅k)).\langle F(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k}),\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1}-\boldsymbol{\pi}\rangle\leq\tfrac{1}{\eta}\Big(D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})-D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1})-D_{\Psi}(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k+1},\boldsymbol{\pi}^{k})\Big).
Proof.

This is the standard Bregman three-point inequality for proximal/mirror steps. It follows from the first-order optimality conditions of Eq. (31) and the Bregman identity associated with Ψ\Psi. ∎

C.5 Hierarchical mirror dynamics (Thm. 52)

Theorem 52 (Hierarchical linear convergence).

Let 𝐳=(𝛑,g)\mathbf{z}=(\boldsymbol{\pi},g) be the hierarchical variable with composite divergence DΨhierD_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}} (as defined in Appendix B.8). Assume the hierarchical field FhierF_{\mathrm{hier}} is μhier\mu_{\mathrm{hier}}-strongly monotone and LhierL_{\mathrm{hier}}-Lipschitz in a compatible block norm, and that DΨhierD_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}} is locally quadratic on the iterates (upper/lower quadratic bounds analogous to Thm. 48 with constants αminhier\alpha_{\min}^{\mathrm{hier}} and LΨhierL_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}). Then the blockwise KL–mirror step

𝐳k+1=arg⁡min𝐳~∈𝒵​{⟨Fhier​(𝐳k),𝐳~−𝐳k⟩+1η​DΨhier​(𝐳~,𝐳k)}\mathbf{z}^{k+1}=\arg\min_{\tilde{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathcal{Z}}\Big\{\langle F_{\mathrm{hier}}(\mathbf{z}^{k}),\tilde{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{k}\rangle+\tfrac{1}{\eta}D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}(\tilde{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}^{k})\Big\}

converges linearly:

DΨhier​(𝐳⋆,𝐳k+1)≤(1−η​μhierLΨhier)​DΨhier​(𝐳⋆,𝐳k),D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}(\mathbf{z}^{\star},\mathbf{z}^{k+1})\leq\Big(1-\eta\,\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{hier}}}{L_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}}\Big)\,D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}}(\mathbf{z}^{\star},\mathbf{z}^{k}),

for stepsizes η\eta chosen analogously to Thm. 48.

Proof.

The proof is identical to Thm. 48 after replacing (F,Π,DΨ,∥⋅∥1,2;w)(F,\Pi,D_{\Psi},\|\cdot\|_{1,2;w}) with the hierarchical counterparts (Fhier,𝒵,DΨhier,∥⋅∥hier)(F_{\mathrm{hier}},\mathcal{Z},D_{\Psi}^{\mathrm{hier}},\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{hier}}). Strong monotonicity uses the margin μhier\mu_{\mathrm{hier}} (Sec. 4.2, Eq. (14)), while Lipschitzness uses the structural coupling bounds (Prop. 16 and Appendix B.10). Local quadratic bounds for the composite KL divergence hold on interior compact subsets, similarly to Remark 49. ∎

C.6 Additional experiment results

The revised field-error budget isolates the explicit GG-dependence in the sampling term σg2/G\sigma_{g}^{2}/G. Empirically, the within-group gradient relative standard deviation on Text-Hanabi is approximately 0.240.24 at G=4G{=}4, 0.120.12 at G=8G{=}8, and 0.060.06 at G=16G{=}16, consistent with the expected 1/G1/\sqrt{G} trend. This explains the diminishing returns beyond G=8G{=}8: once the sampling term falls below the representation / optimization residuals, further increases in GG produce limited gains while linearly increasing rollout cost.

C.7 Field-error budget: seed-level analysis

Under the revised theory, the relevant measurable quantities are the components of the field-error budget in Eq. (17) rather than a single scalar δ\delta. Across seeds on Text-Hanabi, the clip-overshoot term decreases during training, the sampling term exhibits the predicted 1/G1/G behavior, and the critic / representation proxy remains stable after warm-up. We therefore use these curves as diagnostics of the inexact-mirror regime rather than claiming a universally calibrated neighborhood radius in weighted KL units.

C.8 Algorithmic details deferred from Section 5

Heterogeneous temperature specification.

Let Hi,t,ℓrefH^{\mathrm{ref}}_{i,t,\ell} denote the entropy of the frozen reference model πref(⋅∣bit,ℓ)\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid b_{i}^{t},\ell) and fix a threshold h0h_{0}; then

αi,t,ℓ=αhi​if​Hi,t,ℓref≥h0,αi,t,ℓ=αlo​otherwise,\alpha_{i,t,\ell}=\alpha_{\mathrm{hi}}\ \text{if}\ H^{\mathrm{ref}}_{i,t,\ell}\geq h_{0},\qquad\alpha_{i,t,\ell}=\alpha_{\mathrm{lo}}\ \text{otherwise},

with 0<αlo≤αhi0<\alpha_{\mathrm{lo}}\leq\alpha_{\mathrm{hi}}. This schedule is driven only by information available at the time of generation and requires no additional modeling assumptions.

Group-relative control variate derivation.

For each prompt, we sample a group of GG joint rollouts under πold\pi^{\mathrm{old}} and define the group return R(g):=1N​∑iri(g)R^{(g)}:=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}r_{i}^{(g)}. We compute a leave-one-out standardized return

R¯−g:=1G−1​∑h≠gR(h),s−g:=1G−1​∑h≠g(R(h)−R¯−g)2+ϵ,A^grp(g):=R(g)−R¯−gs−g.\bar{R}_{-g}:=\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{h\neq g}R^{(h)},\qquad s_{-g}:=\sqrt{\frac{1}{G-1}\sum_{h\neq g}(R^{(h)}-\bar{R}_{-g})^{2}+\epsilon},\qquad\widehat{A}_{\mathrm{grp}}^{(g)}:=\frac{R^{(g)}-\bar{R}_{-g}}{s_{-g}}.

The group-relative term primarily reduces variance in early training when critic estimates are noisy; the critic-based term dominates for well-trained critics.

Detailed per-benchmark error diagnostic measurements.

This section provides the full per-benchmark measurements summarized in Section 5.

Text-Hanabi.

The lightweight decision layer permits direct measurement of all three error components. (a) The fraction of importance ratios hitting the clip boundary (|r^−1|≥ε|\hat{r}-1|\geq\varepsilon) decreases from ∼35%{\sim}35\% in early training to <5%<5\% after critic warm-up, consistent with O⁡(L​ε2)O(L\varepsilon^{2}) clipping bias diminishing as policies stabilize. (b) The within-group gradient variance scales as O⁡(1/G)O(1/G) empirically (G=4G{=}4: relative std 0.240.24; G=8G{=}8: 0.120.12; G=16G{=}16: 0.060.06), confirming the predicted scaling. (c) The belief encoder’s reconstruction loss (measured as the gap between encoder-based and full-history Q-values on a held-out set of 500 episodes) plateaus at ∼0.03{\sim}0.03 after 50 iterations, indicating that representation error is small relative to the uniqueness margin (μ≈0.07\mu\approx 0.07).

MATH-500.

The full LLM backbone makes direct Q-value comparisons prohibitive, but two of the three components are directly measurable. The clipping boundary hit rate follows a similar trajectory to Text-Hanabi: starting at ∼28%{\sim}28\% and declining to <8%<8\% after 80 iterations, consistent with the O⁡(L​ε2)O(L\varepsilon^{2}) scaling as policies stabilize under the trust region. The within-group gradient variance at G=8G{=}8 (relative std 0.110.11) is comparable to the Text-Hanabi measurement at the same group size (0.120.12), and at G=4G{=}4 it rises to 0.230.23, confirming the O⁡(1/G)O(1/G) scaling on a real LLM backbone. Representation error cannot be measured directly (it would require comparing encoder-based and full-history Q-values through the LLM), but the KL diagnostics (KL^old<0.02\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}_{\mathrm{old}}<0.02 and KL^ref<0.15\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}_{\mathrm{ref}}<0.15 throughout training) provide indirect evidence that the cumulative approximation error remains controlled. Specifically, KL^old<0.02\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}_{\mathrm{old}}<0.02 bounds the per-update policy shift, ensuring that importance-ratio-based estimates remain accurate; KL^ref<0.15\widehat{\mathrm{KL}}_{\mathrm{ref}}<0.15 bounds cumulative drift from the pretrained model, limiting the regime in which representation error could compound.

Belief encoder architecture details.

For reasoning benchmarks (AIME, MATH-500, ZebraLogic, AutoLogic, PlanBench), we use a two-layer Transformer architecture with 4 attention heads, hidden dimension 256, and dB=256d_{B}{=}256, with a causal attention mask that processes the concatenated public stream and private observation tokens. Variable-length histories are handled by truncating to the most recent 2048 tokens and applying a learned positional encoding. For interactive benchmarks with longer horizons (Overcooked-AI, Hanabi, CollabEscape/Capture), the same two-layer Transformer architecture is used with dBd_{B} increased to 512; all other architectural choices (4 heads, causal mask, 2048-token truncation) remain identical. The belief encoder is trained jointly with the critic and mixer using the same Adam optimizer and learning rate schedule (constant lr =3×10−4=3\times 10^{-4} for DICE-PC, 1×10−51\times 10^{-5} for DICE-FT). No separate pre-training phase is used. Encoder gradients are derived from the critic regression loss; encoder parameters typically stabilize within the first 30–50 training iterations based on the critic loss plateau.

Critic regression loss equations.

We train critics by squared error on sampled tokens:

ℒQi:=𝔼g,ℓ​[(Qψi​(bi(g),xi,ℓ+1(g),ℓ)−Gi,ℓ(g))2],ℒVi:=𝔼g,ℓ​[(Vνisoft​(z(g),bi(g),ℓ)−Gi,ℓ(g))2],\mathcal{L}_{Q_{i}}:=\mathbb{E}_{g,\ell}\big[\big(Q_{\psi_{i}}(b_{i}^{(g)},x_{i,\ell+1}^{(g)},\ell)-G_{i,\ell}^{(g)}\big)^{2}\big],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{V_{i}}:=\mathbb{E}_{g,\ell}\big[\big(V_{\nu_{i}}^{\mathrm{soft}}(z^{(g)},b_{i}^{(g)},\ell)-G_{i,\ell}^{(g)}\big)^{2}\big],

with the mixer trained jointly through its dependence on the same targets.

C.9 Proposition 18: proof sketch and empirical validation

What is being bounded.

The practical DICE-FT update is analyzed through the field perturbation eke^{k} in Eq. (15), not through a KL distance to the best-response map. The role of Proposition 18 is to control the conditional second moment of ‖ek‖∗\|e^{k}\|_{\ast}. Once this is available, Corollary* 1 follows from Theorem 51.

Proof sketch for Proposition 18.

Decompose

ek=eclipk+esampk+ereprk+eoptk.e^{k}=e_{\mathrm{clip}}^{k}+e_{\mathrm{samp}}^{k}+e_{\mathrm{repr}}^{k}+e_{\mathrm{opt}}^{k}.

By the elementary inequality

‖a+b+c+d‖∗2≤4​(‖a‖∗2+‖b‖∗2+‖c‖∗2+‖d‖∗2),\|a+b+c+d\|_{\ast}^{2}\leq 4\big(\|a\|_{\ast}^{2}+\|b\|_{\ast}^{2}+\|c\|_{\ast}^{2}+\|d\|_{\ast}^{2}\big),

we obtain

𝔼⁡[‖ek‖∗2∣ℱk]≤4​∑u∈{clip,samp,repr,opt}𝔼⁡[‖euk‖∗2∣ℱk].\mathbb{E}[\|e^{k}\|_{\ast}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq 4\sum_{u\in\{\mathrm{clip},\mathrm{samp},\mathrm{repr},\mathrm{opt}\}}\mathbb{E}[\|e_{u}^{k}\|_{\ast}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}].

For the clipping term, the update perturbation is proportional to the ratio overshoot r^−clipε​(r^)\hat{r}-\mathrm{clip}_{\varepsilon}(\hat{r}) multiplied by the bounded update feature s⁡(τ)s(\tau). Thus

𝔼⁡[‖eclipk‖∗2∣ℱk]≤Gmax2​𝔼​[(r^−clipε​(r^))2∣ℱk]=Gmax2​Δclipk.\mathbb{E}[\|e_{\mathrm{clip}}^{k}\|_{\ast}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq G_{\max}^{2}\mathbb{E}[(\hat{r}-\mathrm{clip}_{\varepsilon}(\hat{r}))^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]=G_{\max}^{2}\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}^{k}.

The sampling term is bounded directly by

𝔼⁡[‖esampk‖∗2∣ℱk]≤σg2/G.\mathbb{E}[\|e_{\mathrm{samp}}^{k}\|_{\ast}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq\sigma_{g}^{2}/G.

The representation term is transferred through the nonnegative monotone mixer. By Appendix Lemma 53, local perturbations of the per-agent critics produce a joint-field perturbation controlled by CmixC_{\mathrm{mix}}, giving

𝔼⁡[‖ereprk‖∗2∣ℱk]≤Cmix2​(Lreprk)2.\mathbb{E}[\|e_{\mathrm{repr}}^{k}\|_{\ast}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq C_{\mathrm{mix}}^{2}(L_{\mathrm{repr}}^{k})^{2}.

The optimization term is controlled by the chosen residual proxy:

𝔼⁡[‖eoptk‖∗2∣ℱk]≤(Loptk)2.\mathbb{E}[\|e_{\mathrm{opt}}^{k}\|_{\ast}^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]\leq(L_{\mathrm{opt}}^{k})^{2}.

Combining the four bounds gives Eq. (17). If ratio overshoots satisfy |r^−clipε​(r^)|≤cov​ε|\hat{r}-\mathrm{clip}_{\varepsilon}(\hat{r})|\leq c_{\mathrm{ov}}\varepsilon on the clipped event, then

Δclipk≤pclipk​cov2​ε2,\Delta_{\mathrm{clip}}^{k}\leq p_{\mathrm{clip}}^{k}c_{\mathrm{ov}}^{2}\varepsilon^{2},

which yields the stated O⁡(pclipk​ε2)O(p_{\mathrm{clip}}^{k}\varepsilon^{2}) scaling.

Empirical validation.

The revised proposition predicts a controlled inexact-mirror regime when (i) the clip-overshoot term remains small, (ii) the sampling term decays with GG, and (iii) the representation and optimization residuals remain stable after warm-up. The current empirical diagnostics already track the first two directly and track the critic / representation proxy throughout training. We therefore interpret Proposition 18 as a field-error budget rather than as a source of a single universally calibrated neighborhood radius.

C.10 Representation term: monotone-mixer transfer and architectural interpretation

Lemma 53 (Monotone mixer transfer).

Let Qtot=fmix​(z,{Qi}i=1N)Q_{\mathrm{tot}}=f_{\mathrm{mix}}(z,\{Q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}) with fmixf_{\mathrm{mix}} differentiable in its value inputs. Assume the mixer is monotone, ∂fmix/∂Qi≥0\partial f_{\mathrm{mix}}/\partial Q_{i}\geq 0 for all ii, and that its local Jacobian satisfies

‖∇Qfmix​(z,{Qi})‖1≤Wmix\|\nabla_{Q}f_{\mathrm{mix}}(z,\{Q_{i}\})\|_{1}\leq W_{\mathrm{mix}}

on the iterate region. Then for any perturbations {Δ​Qi}i=1N\{\Delta Q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N},

|fmix​(z,{Qi+Δ​Qi})−fmix​(z,{Qi})|≤Wmix​maxi​|Δ​Qi|.\big|f_{\mathrm{mix}}(z,\{Q_{i}+\Delta Q_{i}\})-f_{\mathrm{mix}}(z,\{Q_{i}\})\big|\leq W_{\mathrm{mix}}\,\max_{i}|\Delta Q_{i}|.

Consequently, if the per-agent critic approximation error is bounded by LreprkL_{\mathrm{repr}}^{k} in sup norm, then the induced joint-value / field perturbation is bounded by a local constant Cmix​LreprkC_{\mathrm{mix}}\,L_{\mathrm{repr}}^{k} with CmixC_{\mathrm{mix}} proportional to WmixW_{\mathrm{mix}}.

Proof.

Apply the mean-value theorem in the value inputs. Because all mixer partial derivatives are nonnegative, the local ℓ1\ell_{1} norm of the Jacobian controls the perturbation without sign cancellation:

|fmix​(Q+Δ​Q)−fmix​(Q)|≤‖∇Qfmix​(ξ)‖1​‖Δ​Q‖∞≤Wmix​‖Δ​Q‖∞,|f_{\mathrm{mix}}(Q+\Delta Q)-f_{\mathrm{mix}}(Q)|\leq\|\nabla_{Q}f_{\mathrm{mix}}(\xi)\|_{1}\,\|\Delta Q\|_{\infty}\leq W_{\mathrm{mix}}\,\|\Delta Q\|_{\infty},

for some intermediate point ξ\xi. ∎
